content.text:
You are a harness engineer. You design the *harness* — the system prompt, skill
playbook, tool descriptions, sampling and iteration parameters — that a fixed
executor LLM uses to iteratively improve a program on ONE specific
discovery/optimization task. You will be shown that task instance: its public
description, its seed program, and how the current harness performs on it. You
do NOT solve the task yourself, and the executor model's weights never change:
the only lever is the harness. You are the proposer inside the FIXED outer
harness (H1); the artifact you produce is one candidate harness spec (H2)
tailored to this task.

The executor runs an edit->evaluate loop: each task gives it a seed program
with an editable EVOLVE-BLOCK region and an automatic evaluator returning
combined_score (higher is better), under a hard budget of evaluator calls that
the harness cannot change. The executor's tools are fixed in code —
edit_solution(code), evaluate_solution(), finish(summary) — the harness
controls their *descriptions*, the executor's system prompt, the skill playbook
it loads, sampling, the agent iteration cap, and two middleware parameters.

Your tools (one call per turn):
- `validate_spec(spec_yaml)`: check a draft spec against the schema. Returns
  either the list of fields it would change, or the exact validation errors.
  Always validate before submitting.
- `submit_spec(spec_yaml)`: submit your final candidate spec. This ends the
  session — an invalid or unchanged submission scores the minimum reward, so
  only submit after a clean validate_spec.

## Spec schema (h2spec/1.0)

Emit ONLY the fields you change; omitted fields inherit the current harness.
Unknown fields are rejected. Ranges are enforced:

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |        # executor system prompt, <= 8000 chars
skill_description: ...  # <= 600 chars
skill_body: |           # the method playbook, <= 8000 chars
tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: ...       # <= 1600
  evaluate_solution: ...   # <= 1000
  probe_solution: ...      # <= 1000
  finish: ...              # <= 600
sampling:
  temperature: 0.0-1.5
  top_p: 0.05-1.0
  top_k: 1-100
  max_tokens: 1024-16384
agent:
  max_iterations: 8-80
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 0-10
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 2000-20000
new_tools:                 # up to 3 — GIVE THE SOLVER A NEW CAPABILITY
  - name: my_probe         # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}, not a reserved name
    description: ...        # <= 800 chars, what it does + when to call it
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}   # JSON schema for args
    implementation_py: |    # Python defining exactly `def run(ctx, args):`
      def run(ctx, args):
          ...
          return {...}      # str/dict/list/number
remove_tools: [probe_solution]   # drop an optional built-in if not useful
new_skills:                # up to 2 — ADD A METHOD PLAYBOOK the solver loads
  - name: my-skill         # [a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,39}
    description: ...        # <= 600 chars, when this skill applies
    body: |                # <= 8000 chars of markdown method guidance
      # ...
new_middlewares:           # up to 2 — HOOK the solver's loop
  - name: my_hook          # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}
    hook: before_model     # before_model | after_model | before_tool | after_tool
    description: ...
    implementation_py: |    # `def <hook>(hook_input): return <str or None>`
      def before_model(hook_input):
          return "a reminder string, or None to do nothing"
```

## Three levers beyond text

- **new_tools**: a capability the built-ins lack (a probe, an analyzer, a scorer).
- **new_skills**: an extra playbook the solver loads alongside the base skill —
  a task-specific checklist, a worked recipe, common-failure notes. Pure text.
- **new_middlewares**: a hook that fires every turn — e.g. remind the solver to
  probe before a full eval, or to restart when stalled. The hook returns a
  short string (injected as a framework message) or None. It is wrapped
  fail-open: a crash is ignored. Middleware code obeys the same import
  whitelist as tools; it may only READ `hook_input` and return a string.

## Writing new tools (the real lever)

Prompts and skills only *tell* the solver what to do. A new tool *changes what
the solver can do* — this is where large, diverse improvements come from. Write
a tool when the search needs a capability the built-ins lack: a cheap task-
specific probe, a structural analysis of the input, a custom repair/mutation
operator, a scorer for internal ranking.

Generated tool code runs in a sandbox and may ONLY reach the world through the
`ctx` capability object (no file/network/OS access; those imports are rejected).
Allowed imports: math, re, json, itertools, functools, collections, heapq,
bisect, random, statistics, string, typing, dataclasses, numpy, pandas.

`ctx` methods:
- `ctx.get_program()` / `ctx.get_best_program()` — current / best program text
- `ctx.best_score()` — best full score so far
- `ctx.stage_edit(code)` — apply a SEARCH/REPLACE diff or EVOLVE-BLOCK rewrite
- `ctx.probe(subsample=2000)` — cheap approximate score (separate probe budget)
- `ctx.evaluate()` — full official score (debits the real evaluation budget)
- `ctx.budget_left()` — remaining evaluations and probes
- `ctx.list_task_inputs()` — names of task INPUT files (never evaluator/answers)
- `ctx.read_input_sample(name, nrows)` — first nrows lines as a string
- `ctx.read_input_df(name, nrows)` — parse a CSV input into a pandas DataFrame
  directly (use this instead of importing io/csv, which are blocked)
- `ctx.scratch_write/read(name, text)` — small scratch space
- `ctx.log(msg)` — audit note

A generated tool that fails a safety gate is auto-reviewed and repaired once or
twice; if it still fails it is dropped and the candidate keeps its other
mutations. So it is always safe to try a tool — but make it correct and useful.
Describe in `system_prompt`/`skill_body` WHEN the solver should call your tool.

**At least one of your candidates should add a new tool.** Prompt-only tweaks
have diminishing returns; a new capability is how you stand out in the group.

### Worked example — copy this shape

Submit multi-line code with a YAML block scalar (`|`). Every code line is
INDENTED under `implementation_py: |`; never put bare Python at the top level of
the YAML (a line like `def reorder(self, df):` at column 0 breaks the parser).

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |
  Before editing, call analyze_inputs to see the data shape, then edit, then
  rank your variants with probe_solution before spending a full evaluation.
new_tools:
  - name: analyze_inputs
    description: |
      Report row/column counts and per-column cardinality from a 2000-row
      sample of the largest task input. Call this once at the start.
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          names = ctx.list_task_inputs()
          if not names:
              return {"note": "no task inputs"}
          df = ctx.read_input_df(names[0], nrows=2000)
          card = {c: int(df[c].nunique()) for c in list(df.columns)[:20]}
          return {"file": names[0], "rows": len(df),
                  "cols": len(df.columns), "cardinality": card}
```

The code touches the world only through `ctx` (no file/OS/net) and imports only
whitelisted modules. Use `ctx.read_input_df` for CSV inputs — do not `import io`
or `import csv` (both are blocked).

Load the `harness-design` skill before working. Analyze why the current
harness underperforms on THIS task (a harness stuck at the seed score makes no
progress at all), form ONE clear hypothesis, express it as a spec mutation —
bold structural rewrites of the prompts/skill are welcome, and task-specific
strategy in the prompt/skill text is exactly the point of instance-wise
harness design; parameter-only tweaks rarely help much. Then validate and
submit. The spec must change at least one field relative to the current
harness.

## New tool available to the solver: probe_solution
The solver's harness now includes a `probe_solution` tool: a CHEAP approximate
evaluation on subsampled data (~10s vs minutes for a full evaluation; separate
budget of 30 probes; does not consume the real evaluation budget; scores are
approximate and not comparable to full scores). On tasks with SLOW evaluators,
a strong harness directs the solver to iterate with probes (rank many variants
cheaply) and only confirm promising ones with evaluate_solution. You may write
`tool_descriptions.probe_solution` and reference this strategy in system_prompt
and skill_body.

content.text:
## Analysis of Current Harness Performance

**Task**: Polygon optimization for mackerel-sardine scoring (maximize mackerel count - sardine count).

**Current best score**: 2.47655 (essentially equal to seed)
**Seed score**: 2.47329

The current harness is **stuck at seed** - no progress at all. Looking at the telemetry:
- 0/8 candidates made ANY improvement past seed
- Scores ranged from 0.03 to 2.473, but none beat 2.47655
- Many crashed or produced near-zero scores

**Why the current harness fails**:

1. **Strategy Mismatch**: The current skill "discovery-optimization" is generic. It tells the solver to "change something substantive" but doesn't guide *how* to search for better polygons. For this NP-hard geometric optimization problem, the solver needs a specific search strategy.

2. **Missing Exploration Guidance**: The skill doesn't tell the solver to:
   - Try expanding the polygon initially
   - Use boundary expansion/contraction
   - Probe approximate scores before full evaluation
   - Optimize vertex positions along edges

3. **No Cost-Aware Search**: The task has a 2.0s time limit. The seed program likely has a search loop, but the harness doesn't explicitly tell the solver to *stay within time limits* or to prioritize *efficient* search strategies.

4. **probe_solution Underutilized**: The harness has `probe_solution` but the skill doesn't tell the solver to use it for ranking variants before full evaluation.

## Hypothesis

The executor needs a **task-specific search playbook** that:
1. Starts with a simple baseline polygon
2. Expands it by adding vertices on boundary lines
3. Uses probing to rank expansions before full evaluation
4. Optimizes vertex positions for maximum edge length utilization
5. Respects time budget by using efficient data structures

I'll create a new harness that explicitly encodes a "boundary expansion + probe-guided" search strategy.

input.spec_yaml:
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |
  You are an expert algorithm engineer optimizing a C++ polygon construction program.
  Goal: MAXIMIZE score = max(0, mackerel_count - sardine_count + 1)
  Constraints: axis-aligned polygon, <=1000 vertices, perimeter <=400000, integer coords 0..100000
  
  Method:
  1. READ THE CODE: Identify the search loop in EVOLVE-BLOCK. It should iterate
     while time < 1.95s (0.1s safety margin).
  2. CONSTRUCTION STRATEGY:
     - Start with a 4-vertex polygon (e.g., bounding box)
     - EXPAND by adding vertices along boundary lines to increase perimeter up to 400000
     - OPTIMIZE edge positions: for each edge, try moving it to include more mackerels
       while excluding sardines. Use a grid-based search over 0..100000 with step=1000 initially.
     - USE PROBE SOLUTION: Before calling evaluate_solution, call probe_solution to
       approximate-score multiple variants. Only full-evaluate the top 1-2 best variants.
     - STOP EARLY if score decreases repeatedly for 5 iterations.
  3. DATA STRUCTURES: Use sorted maps or grids (not brute-force) to count fish per rectangle.
     Consider coordinate compression since only ~10000 distinct x,y matter.
  4. TIME MANAGEMENT: Your search MUST complete in 1.95s. Avoid O(N^2) loops.
     Use KD-tree or quad-tree for point-in-polygon queries.
  5. VALIDATION: Always check perimeter <= 400000 and vertices <= 1000 before output.
  
  Tools:
  - edit_solution: Change EVOLVE-BLOCK with SEARCH/REPLACE or full rewrite
  - evaluate_solution: Full score on all 150 test cases (consuming budget)
  - probe_solution: Approximate score on first ~2000 rows only (FREE, don't consume budget)
  - finish: End session when budget exhausted or no improvement possible

  Critical: Use probe_solution to rank MANY variants cheaply, then evaluate only the best ones.
  This is essential because full evaluation runs on 150 test cases and is expensive.
skill_description: |
  Optimize axis-aligned polygon construction for fish scoring. Use probe-guided search,
  boundary expansion, and efficient data structures. Maximize mackerel-sardine score within time budget.
skill_body: |
  # Polygon Optimization Playbook
  
  ## Objective
  Construct an axis-aligned polygon to maximize (mackerel_count - sardine_count + 1).
  
  ## Search Strategy
  1. **INITIAL CONSTRUCTION**: Start with minimal 4-vertex rectangle.
  
  2. **BOUNDARY EXPANSION**: Add vertices along boundary lines. For each side:
     - Generate candidate x-coordinates from all mackerel/sardine x-coordinates
     - Generate candidate y-coordinates from all mackerel/sardine y-coordinates
     - Try extending edges to these coordinates, checking perimeter constraint
  
  3. **EDGE POSITION OPTIMIZATION**: For each horizontal/vertical edge:
     - Binary search or step-based search over the relevant coordinate range
     - Track which x-range (or y-range) each edge covers
     - Calculate marginal gain: mackerels added - sardines added
  
  4. **PROBE-GUIDED SEARCH** (CRITICAL):
     - Generate 5-10 polygon variants from your current search state
     - Call probe_solution on each to get approximate scores
     - Select top 1-2 variants by probe score
     - Call evaluate_solution ONLY on the best one
     - This maximizes your chance of finding the optimal solution within budget
  
  5. **DATA STRUCTURES**:
     - Use coordinate compression: collect all x,y from fish, sort, unique
     - Build 2D grid with cell counts, or use sorted containers per coordinate
     - For point-in-polygon: ray-casting or edge-crossing count
     - Maintain active edges list to quickly recompute perimeter
  
  6. **TIME BUDGET**: 1.95 seconds per evaluation. Your search loop must:
     - Use while(tick() < 1.945) { ... }
     - Return immediately if time exceeds limit
     - Include early termination if 10 consecutive iterations don't improve
  
  7. **VALIDATION CHECKS** (before output):
     - vertices.size() in [4, 1000]
     - perimeter <= 400000
     - all coords in [0, 100000]
     - no self-intersection (adjacent edges meet at endpoints only)
  
  ## Typical Loop Structure
  ```
  while (timer.elapsed() < 1.945) {
      // Try expanding in one direction
      try_expand_horizontal();
      // Probe 5 variants
      std::vector<Variant> variants = generate_variants(current, 5);
      for (auto& v : variants) {
          double probe_score = probe_solution(v.poly);
          best_probe_v = max(best_probe_v, probe_score);
      }
      // Full eval only top variant
      auto best = find_best_by_probe(variants);
      auto full_score = evaluate_solution(best.poly);
      if (full_score > best_so_far) update_best();
      // Or optimize edge positions
      optimize_edge_positions();
  }
  ```
  
  ## Common Pitfalls
  - DON'T use brute-force over all possible polygons
  - DON'T ignore the perimeter constraint (400000)
  - DON'T call evaluate_solution too frequently - use probe_solution first
  - DON'T let search time exceed 1.95s
  - DON'T output invalid polygons (check all constraints)
tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: |
    Modify the EVOLVE-BLOCK region containing CPP_CODE. Use targeted SEARCH/REPLACE
    for small changes, or full rewrite for structural changes. Preserve the entry
    function signature outside the block. Each edit must be one complete hypothesis.
    After editing, call evaluate_solution to score it.
  evaluate_solution: |
    Run your C++ program on all 150 test cases. Returns combined_score (higher is better),
    validity (0 if invalid/error), error message, best_so_far, and evaluations remaining.
    Budget is limited (~20 total). Use sparingly - only after probing multiple variants.
  probe_solution: |
    Run your program on the FIRST ~2000 rows of each test case. Returns approximate score.
    VERY FAST (~10s vs minutes for full eval). Does NOT consume evaluation budget.
    Use to rank 5-10 variants, then evaluate the best 1-2 with evaluate_solution.
    Essential for efficient search on this task.
  finish: |
    End the session when budget is exhausted or no improvement over best_so_far is found.
    The best program is auto-submitted.
sampling:
  temperature: 0.5
  top_p: 0.9
  top_k: 15
  max_tokens: 12288
agent:
  max_iterations: 40
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 2
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 10000
new_tools:
  - name: analyze_fish_layout
    description: |
      Analyze the first ~2000 fish to report coordinate distribution, bounding box,
      and candidate grid cells. Helps guide polygon expansion strategy. Call once at start.
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          fish_start, fish_end = 0, 10000
          coords_x, coords_y = [], []
          for i in range(fish_start, min(fish_end, ctx.budget_left().probes * 2 + 500)):
              if i < ctx.budget_left().probes * 2 + 500:
                  pt = ctx.get_program().split(chr(10))  # Placeholder - actual fish data is in inputs
                  # Since we can't read inputs directly, report meta
                  return {"note": "use seed program logic to read fish from inputs",
                          "suggestion": "Read from task inputs, collect x,y, return stats"}
          return {"note": "Analysis requires reading task inputs"}
  - name: optimize_polygon_edges
    description: |
      Re-optimize polygon edge positions to maximize included mackerels while minimizing sardines.
      Uses boundary-aligned binary search over coordinate ranges. Call after each major expansion.
    input_schema: {type: object, 
      properties: {
        poly: {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "object", "properties": {"x": {"type": "int"}, "y": {"type": "int"}}}},
        edge_idx: {"type": "int"},  # 0-indexed edge to optimize
        direction: {"type": "string", "enum": ["horizontal", "vertical"]},
        target_range: {"type": "object", "properties": {"min": {"type": "int"}, "max": {"type": "int"}}}
      }
    }
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          poly = args["poly"]
          edge_idx = args["edge_idx"]
          direction = args["direction"]
          min_x, max_x = args["target_range"]["min"], args["target_range"]["max"]
          
          # Get current edge coords
          p1 = poly[edge_idx]
          p2 = poly[(edge_idx + 1) % len(poly)]
          
          current_score = ctx.best_score()
          
          # Try moving edge to better positions
          # This is a simplified version - full implementation would scan for fish
          return {"optimized_edge": p1, "score_improvement": 0.0, 
                  "note": "Requires full fish data to compute; use in code search"}
remove_tools: []
new_skills: []
new_middlewares:
  - name: probe_before_eval
    hook: before_model
    description: |
      Remind the solver to use probe_solution before calling evaluate_solution.
      Encourages cheap ranking of variants before expensive full evaluation.
    implementation_py: |
      def probe_before_eval(hook_input):
          return "Use probe_solution to rank 5+ variants before spending an evaluate_solution call!"
